sections.h2: What matters most when selling a house in Livingston, NJ?
sections.html:
Livingston is a high-value Essex County township, so the biggest costs in a sale are usually the price-based state fees and any repairs a buyer's inspector flags. The local paperwork is short: a smoke detector certification from the fire department and a check for open building permits. Everything else is the deed, the state fee schedule and the Essex County recording office.

The township has 13.79 square miles of land and 32,223 residents in the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate, up from 31,330 in 2020. Its 2020 count of 31,330 was the highest the township has recorded.

sections.h2: What is Livingston's history and layout?
sections.html:
Settlers from Newark negotiated for the Horseneck Tract in 1699, and disputes over land titles led to the Horseneck Riots between 1745 and 1755. The township was incorporated on February 5, 1813 from parts of Caldwell and Springfield townships, and it was named for William Livingston, the first governor of New Jersey. Fairmount (now part of West Orange) split off in 1862 and Roseland in 1908.

The town grew slowly until automobiles arrived. Mount Pleasant Avenue, one of the first turnpikes in the state, was once the main access. The population rose from 5,972 in 1940 to 23,124 in 1960 and peaked near 30,127 in 1970 before settling in the 26,000 to 28,000 range, then climbing back to 31,330 by 2020.

Livingston sits in southwestern Essex County, bordered by Roseland to the north, West Orange to the east, Millburn and Short Hills to the south, and Florham Park and East Hanover in Morris County to the west. The Passaic River marks the western edge. Place names buyers use include Cheapside, Northfield, Washington Place, West Livingston and Cedar Ridge.

sections.h2: How expensive are Livingston homes compared with local incomes?
sections.html:
Nearly nine in ten homes are owner-occupied, and the median owner-occupied value for 2020 to 2024 is $821,100. At that value a typical sale reaches one of the upper brackets of the state fee schedule.

sections.h2: How do schools, hospitals and parks affect Livingston homes?
sections.html:
Schools are the first filter for most buyers. Livingston Public Schools have six elementary schools (Burnet Hill, Collins, Harrison, Hillside, Mount Pleasant and Riker Hill), Mount Pleasant Middle School for grade 6, Heritage Middle School for grades 7 and 8, and Livingston High School, which received a National Blue Ribbon award in 1997-98. The district had 6,151 students in 2019-20.

Cooperman Barnabas Medical Center, a 597-bed hospital established in 1865, sits in the south of town. More than 470 acres of wooded parkland has hiking trails, and roughly a quarter of the township's land stays in a natural state. Riker Hill Complex is a 204-acre park on the township's edge.

Retail is changing. The Livingston Mall at the southwest corner has lost several anchors, and the Route 10 corridor and the Livingston Avenue center, including the Livingston Town Center mixed-use project, carry more everyday shopping. Office parks along Eisenhower Parkway house companies such as CoreWeave and a Verizon customer service center.

sections.h2: How do residents get to New York and Newark from Livingston?
sections.html:
The township is 21.9 miles from New York City, and rail service runs through stations in neighboring communities. Options buyers compare:

  • Highways: Interstate 280 and Route 10 cross the town, and I-80, the Garden State Parkway and the New Jersey Turnpike connect through I-280.
  • Bus to Manhattan: the Community Coach 77 route reaches the Port Authority Bus Terminal, and OurBus runs a commuter route serving Livingston and West Orange.
  • Bus to Newark: NJ Transit routes 70, 71 and 73, with local route 873.
  • Rail: Morristown Line stations in Short Hills, Millburn and South Orange sit 5 to 7 miles away, and the fee-based Livingston Express Shuttle makes a 15-minute run between Livingston Mall and South Orange Station.

sections.h2: Does Livingston require a certificate of occupancy to sell a house?
sections.html:
No. The township's own FAQ says a certificate of occupancy is not required to sell a home. It does suggest calling the Building Department at 973-992-5000, extension 5200, to find out whether open permits exist on the property, and to do that well before the closing date because open permits can slow a sale.

You will need a smoke detector certification. Call the Livingston Fire Department at 973-992-2373 to get it. The Fire Prevention Bureau also inspects residential occupancies when they are resold or when a rental changes occupants, and it enforces the state fire code for smoke and carbon monoxide detectors. The Building Department is at 357 S. Livingston Avenue, second floor.

  • Replacing a sink, toilet or tub in the same spot needs no permit, but moving fixtures does.
  • New electrical or plumbing work needs a permit even when you only swap cabinets.
  • A shed over 200 square feet needs a building permit and zoning approval, and a smaller one needs zoning approval.
  • A fence around a pool, spa or hot tub needs a building permit.

sections.h2: What fees come due at a Livingston closing?
sections.html:
The seller pays the state realty transfer fee when the deed is recorded. A $821,100 sale falls into the over-$350,000 schedule, which charges $2.90 per $500 on the first $150,000, $4.25 per $500 from $150,000 to $200,000, $4.80 per $500 from $200,000 to $550,000 and $5.30 per $500 from $550,000 to $850,000.

If the price tops $1 million, a graduated fee applies to residential deeds: 1% of the total price between $1 million and $2 million, 2% up to $2.5 million, 2.5% up to $3 million, 3% up to $3.5 million and 3.5% above that. The seller is responsible for it, and a deed over $1 million has to carry the state's affidavit form. Run the number before you accept an offer close to that line.

Deeds are recorded with the Essex County Register of Deeds and Mortgages, which records property transactions for all 22 municipalities in the county and holds a copy of every deed and mortgage recorded since 1637. Ask the Register for its current address and hours before you send documents, or let your closing attorney or title company handle it.

sections.h2: Should I list or sell a Livingston house as-is for cash?
sections.html:
With values above $800,000, a listing often pays more when a house is updated and shows well, because owner-occupants make up most of the housing stock. An as-is sale makes more sense when the house needs a roof, kitchen or systems work, when you must move on a fixed date, or when you inherited the property and want a quick close.

Compare offers on net proceeds, not headline price. Count the transfer fee, any repairs a buyer will request, carrying costs while the house is listed, and who handles the smoke certification. Get each offer in writing before you choose.

faqs.q: Do I need a certificate of occupancy to sell my house in Livingston?
faqs.a: No. The township says a certificate of occupancy is not required for a sale. You do need a smoke detector certification from the fire department, and the township suggests checking with the Building Department for open permits well before closing.

faqs.q: How do I get the smoke detector certification in Livingston?
faqs.a: Call the Livingston Fire Department at 973-992-2373. The Fire Prevention Bureau handles smoke and carbon monoxide detector compliance for residential resales.

faqs.q: Who pays the realty transfer fee in Livingston?
faqs.a: The seller. It is based on the price recited in the deed and collected when the deed is recorded. Sales above $1 million also carry a graduated percent fee that the seller owes.

faqs.q: Where is a Livingston deed recorded?
faqs.a: With the Essex County Register of Deeds and Mortgages, which records property transactions for all 22 municipalities in Essex County. Your attorney or title company normally files it.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Livingston house with an unpermitted addition?
faqs.a: Yes, but expect questions. Call the Building Department at 973-992-5000, extension 5200, to learn what is on file. A buyer's lender or attorney may ask for the work to be permitted or priced into the offer.
